videos.title: Meta Muse Is Incredible - 5 Features You Need To Try
videos.ai_tech_id: Meta Muse (Meta) — general-purpose AI agent app
summary: Paul J Lipsky, in a video sponsored by WhisPrompt, gives Meta Muse a strong endorsement, calling it one of the easiest AI agents he's used despite a simple interface that undersells how much it can actually do, and sets up a tour of five standout use cases plus its free usage limits.

He walks through Muse acting as a personal shopper that tracks down items across the web, demonstrates pairing it with the sponsor tool WhisPrompt, and shows off its voice-response mode and its ability to generate custom podcast episodes on a topic of the user's choosing.

The video closes on two more capability-heavy features — Muse placing phone calls on the user's behalf and taking remote access of a computer to complete tasks — before breaking down how generous the app's free tier currently is, framing Muse as unusually capable for a no-cost AI agent.

videos.title: No, Seriously. Claude Code is Starting To Get Dangerous
videos.ai_tech_id: Claude Code (Anthropic) — agentic coding tool risk and governance
summary: Nate Herk opens by insisting his warning about Claude Code isn't fearmongering, then uses Anthropic's recent decision to shut down one of its own models as a jumping-off point for a broader argument that agentic coding tools are becoming powerful enough to carry real business risk.

He points to a bug that went unnoticed for days as evidence that autonomous coding agents can quietly cause damage before anyone catches it, and extends the discussion into predictions about how AI will reshape classrooms, cybersecurity practices, and government regulation, floating comparisons to arms-control-style oversight.

The video ends on three skills Nate argues matter most as agentic AI improves — correctly identifying the real underlying business problem before automating it, tightly controlling what systems and data an agent can access, and taking personal responsibility for whatever an agent produces — framing accountability as the piece most people are currently getting wrong.

videos.title: 5 ChatGPT Power Words for Visual Answers
videos.ai_tech_id: ChatGPT (OpenAI) — slash-command prompting for visual output formats
summary: Sabrina Ramonov introduces five "power word" slash commands that tell ChatGPT to reformat any topic into a specific visual layout rather than plain text, positioning them as a quick way to make ChatGPT answers easier to absorb.

She runs through the five commands and what each produces: /timelineview for a chronological visual timeline, /anime-explainer for turning a topic into an anime-style story, /visualcheatsheet for a one-page reference sheet, /explodedview for a schematic breaking an object or concept into its parts, and /mindmap for a diagram of how ideas connect.

The video closes with guidance on when to reach for each command — timelines for sequence-dependent topics, anime explainers for memorability, cheat sheets for studying, exploded views for dissecting components, and mind maps for relational ideas — and encourages viewers to save the list of exact commands for reuse.

videos.title: 5 ChatGPT Visual Codes for Timelines, Mind Maps, and Study Guides
videos.ai_tech_id: ChatGPT (OpenAI) — slash-command prompting for visual output formats
summary: Sabrina Ramonov revisits the same five ChatGPT visual slash-command formats covered in her earlier video the same day, reframing them as "visual codes" that convert a single topic into a timeline, mind map, cheat sheet, anime explainer, or schematic depending on which command is typed.

She again lists the five exact commands — /anime-explainer, /timelineview, /mindmap, /visualcheatsheet, and /explodedview — describing each as returning a distinct visual format so the user can pick the view that best fits what they're trying to learn.

The video repeats the situational guidance on when each format helps most, and adds a call to action pointing viewers to her paid resource for hundreds of additional ChatGPT "secret codes," positioning this video as a companion piece to the earlier upload rather than new material.
